questions.q: What does it mean that model loss follows a "power law" with respect to parameter count?
options: Loss increases as parameter count increases
Loss is unrelated to parameter count beyond a certain size
On log-log axes, loss vs. parameter count falls close to a straight line, with no plateau across many orders of magnitude
Loss decreases linearly for every additional parameter
questions.explain: A power-law relationship appears as a straight line when both axes are log-scaled. Kaplan et al. found this held across many orders of magnitude without an obvious plateau.

questions.q: In the Kaplan et al. (2020) framing, what do N, D, and C represent?
options: Three stages of the training pipeline: cleaning, dedup, and mixing
Three different model architectures being compared
Three evaluation benchmarks
Parameter count, dataset size (tokens), and compute (FLOPs)
questions.explain: N is non-embedding parameter count, D is dataset size in tokens, and C is compute, approximately 6 · N · D FLOPs for one pass over the data.

questions.q: Why do small exponents in the scaling-law power law matter practically?
options: They are irrelevant to training decisions
They mean returns to scale are real but diminishing -- a 10x increase buys a smaller gain than the previous 10x
They mean scaling never produces any improvement
They mean the model will overfit immediately
questions.explain: The exponents observed are small (well under 1), so loss keeps improving with scale, but each additional order of magnitude yields a smaller improvement than the one before.

questions.q: Why do teams fit scaling laws using small, cheap training runs instead of only the final large run?
options: Large runs can cost millions of dollars, so teams extrapolate from a cheap size ladder to predict the large run's loss before committing the budget
Small runs are required by law for AI safety compliance
Scaling laws cannot be fit on large models at all
Small models always outperform large ones
questions.explain: Training many full-scale candidates is prohibitively expensive, so teams fit the power-law curve on a ladder of cheap, small runs and extrapolate to the target scale.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of scaling laws as a planning tool?
options: They perfectly predict every downstream capability, including emergent ones
They predict pretraining loss, but some capabilities emerge abruptly at a scale threshold rather than improving smoothly, and extrapolating far outside the studied range carries risk
They eliminate the need for any evaluation after training
They only apply to image models, not language models
questions.explain: Scaling laws are strong predictors of loss within studied ranges, but downstream task performance and emergent behaviors don't always track loss smoothly, and extrapolation has limits.
